processing: Steamed, rolled and dried in the usual Japanese sencha way; the area's identity comes from its mountain growing conditions rather than a special method.
harvest_season: First flush in mountain gardens typically runs from late April into early May, and it is the prized picking.
appearance_dry: Typical of mountain sencha: slender, dark green needles.
appearance_liquor: Clear pale yellow-green, as is usual for regular-steamed sencha.
appearance_wet: Bright green, mostly whole leaf, as with other sencha of this type.
taste_profile: Described locally as fragrant and refined, with a clean, crisp taste and an easy finish.

brewing.notes: Usual sencha guidance: water around 70 to 80 C, and pour every last drop so the second steep stays lively.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring tea, with shincha from the first picking appearing around May, as is usual in Shizuoka. Drink within about a year. Sub-area names such as Haruno and Tatsuyama also appear on packs.
description:
Tenryu-cha comes from the Tenryu ward of Hamamatsu, the forested northern part of the city, around nine-tenths of it woodland. This is mountain tea, grown in a very different setting from the flat, sunny plantations further south.

The distinction is climate: morning fog and big swings between day and night temperatures along the Tenryu River. Processing is sencha as Shizuoka usually makes it, so what you are paying for is the garden.

Expect aroma first, then a clean, crisp taste and a smooth swallow, which is how the prefecture and the city both describe it. Treat it as sencha: moderately hot water and a short steep, with no need to push it.

Buy it fresh, from the current spring. Tea from the plateau south of the city is sold separately as Hamamatsu tea, so do not assume the two are the same; Haruno and Tatsuyama are named areas within Tenryu.
history:
Hamamatsu City describes Tenryu as a long-established high-grade tea area, with tea farming active since the Meiji era. The prefecture notes numerous awards at the national tea competition, including area prizes.

Much beyond this, including a formal boundary for the name, is not clearly recorded.
